newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Insolvent Maculan cuts equity, prevents probe.
newsitem.headline: Insolvent Maculan cuts equity, prevents probe.

text.p: Shareowners of insolvent Austrian construction holding Maculan on Tuesday agreed to a 15-to-one capital write-down and a subsequent capital increase to avoid bankruptcy for what was once the country's top building firm.

Maculan Holding was forced into insolvency in February with 12 billion schillings ($1.1 billion) in debts after racking up huge losses in its sprawling east German operations. Most of its operative units have since been sold off.

The write-down will cut the holding's equity to 27 million schillings, from 404.25 million previously. The Holding's new majority owner, privately owned Leitl/Rieder group, will be excluded from a subsequent capital increase to 59.3 million.
"If there's a bankruptcy, creditors and shareholders will get zero," acting chief executive and majority owner Alexander Maculan told angry shareholders at an annual general meeting.
If the holding manages to complete its insolvency proceedings and avoid bankruptcy, creditors would by law be guaranteed a payout of at least 20 percent on their claims.
Maculan voted down a demand by shareholders to ask a consultancy to launch an investigation into alleged management failures that may have pushed the group over the brink.

Insolvency administrator Nikolaus Reining told shareholders the costs of such a probe would endanger the holding's chances of avoiding bankruptcy and may even prompt Leitl/Rieder to reconsider its acquisition of a controlling stake in the group.
Maculan Holding's sales fell to 941 million schillings last year after the sale of most of its units from 15.6 billion a year ago. Total losses were put at five billion schillings.

The group's collapse was the biggest failure of a listed company in Austria since World War Two and the first to hit the blue-chip ATX index, from which Maculan's shares were dropped in May. Maculan himself was voted "Manager of the Year" by an Austrian business weekly in 1994.
